ai.headline: Prince Harry says he wants to mend ties with King Charles and William
ai.summary: Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, has said he hopes to repair his strained relationship with his father, King Charles, and his brother, Prince William. In an interview with GQ magazine conducted in New York, he described family rifts as a common experience many people can relate to, and said reconciling was the most important goal. He also said he has no interest in sympathy, crediting his own therapy and support network for helping him cope with grief after his mother's death.\n\n Harry also explained why his family moved back to the United Kingdom, citing opportunities for the family and the chance for his children, Archie and Lilibet, to attend British schools. The GQ interview was released as the royal family hosted the Sultan of Oman at Windsor Castle for a state visit. A spokesperson for the Sussex household later said his remarks were not aimed at William or any other royal, and were offered in a broader sense.
key_points: Harry told GQ he wants to reconcile with King Charles and Prince William.
He called family disputes a widely relatable issue and said he wants his own to be resolved.

ai.headline: Meta reports Q3 results as a New Mexico $25 billion penalty lands
ai.summary:
Interest in Meta stock is rising around two developments that landed on the same day. Meta was scheduled to release its third-quarter results after the market closed on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, the first major report of Big Tech's earnings season. Analysts polled by Bloomberg expected earnings of about $3.56 per share and revenue near $63.3 billion, compared with $1.05 per share and $51.2 billion a year earlier. Capital spending was projected to rise roughly 117% to $41 billion, and Reality Labs was expected to post an operating loss of about $5.2 billion. Investors are watching closely because Meta is one of the largest AI spenders, and Bloomberg reported that a weak result could add to existing worries about the AI trade.

Separately, a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties, according to a court filing reported by CNBC. The case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal and a September jury finding that the company misled state residents about data privacy and the handling of harmful content. The jury counted more than 43 million violations under the state's unfair practices law, with a maximum of $5,000 each, but the judge set the final amount, which was reduced from a much larger figure the filing cited. The judge also said interest would accrue at 15% a year until the fine is paid. CNBC said it had contacted Meta for comment, and the company's response was not reported in the sources reviewed.
key_points: Meta was set to report third-quarter 2026 results after the close on Wednesday, October 21.
Bloomberg analyst consensus expected about $3.56 EPS and $63.3 billion in revenue, versus $1.05 and $51.2 billion a year earlier.
Projected capital expenditures were about $41 billion, up roughly 117% year over year.
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion over privacy and consumer-protection violations, according to CNBC.
The penalty is tied to the Cambridge Analytica scandal; the judge set interest at 15% a year until paid.
ai.unknown: It is not yet clear how Meta will respond to the $25 billion penalty, whether it will appeal, or how the quarterly results will be received by investors.

ai.summary:

Suzuki managed the team for one season, which ended with the franchise's first 100-loss campaign. The organization offered him a special assistant role instead, and it plans to hire a new manager and coaching staff.

Interim general manager John Mozeliak had earlier said he hoped to keep Suzuki, but he noted that the decision would rest with incoming ownership. Kroenke Sports & Entertainment is expected to finalize its purchase of the club in early 2027. Mozeliak has said Suzuki earned respect in the clubhouse, though he also said the team's record did not fully reflect Suzuki's ability. Suzuki, 43, is the first Hawaiian-born manager in MLB history, according to MLB.com. Several outlets, including ESPN and CBS Sports, reported the decision as well. It is still unclear whether Mozeliak will remain as GM when his contract expires in December.

ai.headline: New Mexico sues Epstein's former lawyer and accountant over alleged cover-up
ai.summary:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a civil lawsuit on Wednesday against Darren Indyke, Jeffrey Epstein's longtime attorney, and Richard Kahn, his longtime accountant. The complaint, filed in federal court in New Mexico, accuses the two men of helping hide Epstein's crimes. It names both men personally and in their roles as co-executors of Epstein's estate. The filing also names the estate itself and a trust that holds its assets. The state wants a court order that would stop the two men from collecting payments from the estate while the case moves forward.

The case centers on Zorro Ranch, Epstein's property in Stanley, New Mexico. According to the complaint, Epstein and his associates abused survivors at the ranch and other locations. The lawsuit also claims the advisers received large salaries and gifts in return for staying silent. Court papers say Indyke received more than $16 million from Epstein and related entities from 2011 to 2019, and Kahn received more than $10 million over that period. Indyke and Kahn have denied knowing about or helping with Epstein's abuse. Their attorney called the suit baseless. Earlier this year, the two men told a House committee they were unaware of Epstein's crimes.
key_points: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed the civil suit in federal court in New Mexico.
The suit accuses Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn of facilitating and concealing Jeffrey Epstein's crimes.
The complaint asks a court to block the two men from receiving estate payments during the case.
The suit alleges Indyke received over $16 million and Kahn over $10 million from Epstein-linked sources between 2011 and 2019.
Indyke and Kahn deny any knowledge of or involvement in the abuse; their lawyers call the suit baseless.
CNN reported that Epstein's will left Indyke $50 million and Kahn $25 million; their attorneys say payments would come only after creditors are paid and probate ends.
ai.unknown: It is unclear how the court will rule on the request to halt estate payments, and the outcome of the separate reported federal investigation of the two men has not been made public.
